blocks.x: Okay Albert, do you want to give your name to start? Albert Giles is my name. This is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins is here too interviewing Albert Giles at 1816 Onzaga Street and the date is June the 15th 1960. Can you tell us just where you were born and the date? Well I was born in Tibidot, Louisiana. Remember your wife has to tell you your birthday. That's all right.
November the 12th. November the 27th. November 27th? That's right. And what year? 1905. Same year I was born. Same year you were born. Well that's wonderful. It was in Tibidot. Can you tell us
anything about your family up there? Your father and your maybe starting with your grandfather if you like. His name and a little bit about him, what instrument he played, what bands he worked with.

Well my grandfather, he was a drummer in the Civil War. I don't know too much about him. I mean I remember him but so far as to sit down and talk with him, I don't know too much about speaking. Sure I understand. I heard that he was a drummer in the old Civil War. Would that have been with the

Confederate Army or what do you think? With a union group that came down, what do you think? Well I wouldn't know. Well the North was fighting the South. Yeah I just wondered though which side, if it was with some of the Louisiana company or if it would be, if it would have joined the union company when they got down here because they got here pretty quick you know I think about the first year of the war. I think it was the Union. Did he play with any other bands, that is any regular other brass bands or you know did he ever talk about
dance music that they had? Well no not in that time I never heard about no dance music.
What was his name by the way? Napoleon Giles.

Yeah. Can you tell us about your father then? My father was named Albert Giles. He was senior and you're junior. Junior. My daddy died when I was around five years old. Do you remember how old he was about then?
He was in his late 30s when he died. Wasn't very old at all. No he was not.

He was a very young man. And I remember he set his drum up once for me. That's one of the things I can never forget that he set the drums up but I was very young. There's not too much I could do. And after he died well I still didn't lose interest because it must have been in me. Because my uncles all they were drummers. The whole family of the brothers was five of them drummers.
All five? That's right. What were their names? I remember the name Clay Giles.
Clay Giles. Oscar Giles. Olivier Giles. And Major Giles. And Albert Giles.
Every one were drummers? All of them was drummers. They all live up in Thibodeau?
Oh that's their home. Thibodeau was their home. They all lived in Thibodeau.
Did they play in a brass band up there? Or what did they play?
Yeah. Well I don't know too much about their life of playing in brass bands there. But I know my daddy did. He played in a brass band. Dad was put up by Joe Gabriel. Thibodeau.
Oh yes. Lewis James told us about that band. I guess you knew him up there too.

Oh that's a relation to me too. Well he's related. I didn't know that's right. That's right. Yeah. There's a little four cousins but they're related. They all played in the same band. Well my uncles, Clay Giles, Oscar Giles, Olivier Giles, where I know of them were playing in brass band was in Yardins. They all moved down here then? That's right. They all moved down. We all had this. And uh, Clay Giles played with the Exoultal Brass band. Oscar Giles played with the old Onward's J.F. band. Also,

I'm gonna put this up here to prevent six kids from interrupting as the wind is blowing against the microphone. Makes the needle jump a little bit. It's nice to have that breeze here on the hot Davidson. That's better now. Okay, excuse me. You were talking about your uncles now?

Yeah. Oliver Giles, he played in the Onward band with Oscar Giles. Oscar Giles played the bass drum and Oliver Giles played the snare drum. And Major Giles, well he played mostly around Thibodeau too. But so far as him playing in any band in Yardins, I don't know anything concerning that. Yeah. Um, this drum set your father had, it was a regular

dance drum set with bass drum and snare and everything? That's right. Set up like they do now in the jazz band? Well, it was a little different. I've heard he made his own foot pedal. Oh yes, in the old days they had one. Yeah.

He didn't have an overhead foot pedal. He had one made in a trap form because it's different in foot pedals. And an overhead foot pedal and a trap foot pedal was made out of wood. But these days they are made out of iron, but they're traps. Yeah. But in those days they were considered as overhead traps. Yeah.
But he made one out of wood. Do you remember, was there a cymbal in the drum set?

Yeah, they had craft cymbals. The Chinese? The craft cymbals, yeah that's right. A Chinese cymbal was called a craft cymbal. He had blocks. Any cowbells like your ears? Yeah, he had cowbells. My bells is not exactly cowbells, they're orchestra bells and his was cowbells at that time. Yeah.
Um, did you just keep your same drum set then that your father had and...
No, my mother got rid of the set that my father had. It was a new leader set. And she got rid of that. And when I come up to play, I got my own set.
Yeah.
And drums.

Did you play up in Thibodeau or when did you move down? How old were you when you moved down to New Orleans? I was about 16 years old. Um, had you played up there? When did you start on drums? I know as you say you started really when you were five years old. I guess you started in your interest in it, but when did you actually start playing it that you could say you were really a drummer?
I started when I was about 17 years old in New Orleans.
After you moved down, you didn't really play drums up there in the group then?
No, I never did play in New Orleans. I mean in Thibodeau I played in New Orleans.
So you moved down here? Did you have lessons when you moved down?

Well when I came down from Thibodeau to New Orleans, I moved with my grandmother. And she lived with her son Oscar Giles. And I told him I thought I had interest that I would like to play a drum. So I worked at the Crescent Steen Partridge Way. I was getting nine dollars a week. I decided I wanted to buy a drum. So he'd take me on Ramport and Padres in a pawn shop. That's where I bought my first set of drums for a second hand. I paid 25 dollars for the set. Things were cheap at that time.
They were a lot cheaper then than them now.

Well I got the set and my Uncle Clay taking me to Old Man Chaloner for lessons. And Old Man Chaloner was a teacher. He didn't only teach you. He made you experience of learning to play instruments. He would have a big band of all of his scholars. On Monday you'd go to lessons. On Wednesday all his scholars would be in the band together. So he taking my Uncle Clay to play the bass drum to give the youngsters ideas about a band being so big. So they brought me over and I would play the snare drum. But they had about 10 or 20 snare drums.
Oh yeah.

And he's such a good teacher if one musician would make a mistake, he could stop the band and pick him out. And he would talk about everybody. Because a blowing instrument, a drum, no care what it was. He would stop the whole band and tell them, hold on, just a minute. Unless you hit that beat again or make that roll again on the drum. Oh no, that's not perfect. Come again and he would hum the beats to you. La, la, la, la, to be sure that you make it perfect. Yeah. He's one of the greatest teachers I think they are.
By the way, where did he live? About where did he teach at his home or any special school? How was it?
He'd teach at his home and he would bring the band to St. Catron Hall.
Well, what on Tulane?
That's right. That's where the band would be when he would have them all together. But he would teach at his home on St. Claude Street.
About where? What's that? Downtown here?
Yeah, St. Claude Street is, you know, around where the Japanese tea garden is in the era? Oh yeah, near St. That's right. That's right. That's right. That's where he lived. Around there.
You remember what he charged for lessons in those days?
Oh yeah, he was charging 25 cents.
25 cents.
25 cents at that time.

Had he played, see we naturally never got to talk to him and I never knew him and don't know much about him. Can you tell us anything about what instruments he played especially well or did he ever work? Do you remember as a musician much?
Yeah, he played dances or anything? I remember he was too old at that time. He had quit playing and retired and he was teaching. He played the trumpet.
Is this his name?
Yeah, yeah. But he could play.
Did he ever say which bands he had been with? Any brass bands or dance bands or did he have his own band? Do you know?
I heard of he had his own brass band. But I never did know the name of it, the brass band, but I heard that he played in old brass band.

Can you tell us anything else about your uncle while I think of it, Clay Giles? Somehow we hear more about him I think than, of course your father died so young. Was your uncle Clay probably the best one of the brothers at Drum then or what would you say?

Well, he was after my father died. But my father, not saying it because it's my father, but I don't know much but what I heard. James can tell you, Joe Gabriel, they played with him. So he was one of the outstanding drummers. He's great. He was a great drummer and he was also a comedian. He had played with shows. And he would get up from the drum and he'd get on the stage.
Oh, an actor and all.
And acting. He was a great buck dancer. At that time buck dancing was great. Tap dancing.
Something like tap dancing.
Without taps on his shoes. Soft shoe dancing, you know. He was a...

Remember any shows that he traveled with? Any certain names? Any of the companies? No. Was it more like vaudeville or would it have been any of the yeah, I think... ...missional shows or anything of that kind? Like some of the...
Mostly it was vaudeville because he was a fella didn't want to travel.
Yeah.

And if shows come in and they found out how good they were they would get him, hire him to play on the show but he never would leave. Yeah. After the show he'd ready to leave well, he never wanted to leave on, you know. As far as he would come from Thibodeau and play in the Orleans, so but to go way off with shows, he never fancied that. He was...
So he did play down here then too, so...
Oh yeah, he played with several of the bands. He played with the old Arnowitz down here like on Carnival Days and Labor Day for the Long Showmans, you know, and brass bands.
Did they have a brass band up there that never had many parades or anything right in Thibodeau that you remember when you were a kid?
Well, yeah, Joe Gabriel. And he had orchestra.
Yeah, I mean, I wondered about the brass band.

Well, he was a violin player and when they had a Kishens or brass band, well, they would form into a brass band. Joe Gabriel would lead the band like a band major. He was a violin player. He didn't play no other instrument, but he would direct them and they would play brass bands.

Can you remember what any of the dance bands were like up there when you were, oh, as far back as you can remember? That is, did it sound like the New Orleans jazz bands here? Was it a different type of music? What would you say? How did it compare?
Well, their band sounded, the orchestra, like old Pierron band.
Oh, yes. Yeah. They made a few records, so we have an idea about how that sounded.
Yeah, well, that's right. He had a band, something on the order.
With the violin and all.
That's right, that's right. That's the kind of band.
About how big was the dance band, if you can remember when you'd hear it?
They had about eight pieces.
About the same size as the ones here.
Yeah, that's right. They had about eight pieces.

Did they ever play any of the old blues up there? Or was it mostly written music? How did you remember? Well, uh, they... For any of the dances, not just the Gabriel Benth, or any other dances around? Any type, what type of music, the pieces that they played? Did they play like waltzes or marches or foxtrotts or quadrilles? Or what kind of music was it like?
They played waltzes, quadrilles, and they played blues, and they played stock music. At that time.
Most of the music they used was written, I mean arranged the stock arrangements that they...

Yeah, they would always arrange it. Today ideas were not as great as the, you would say, the modern arrangement, that they would arrange it, that they could play it and they would always play it. That way they had the feelings of playing their music. Yeah.
They played the St. Louis Blues.
And I recall that they played a blues they called Ho, Alley Ho. I don't know if you ever heard of that.
You've never heard of that?
Yeah, well, that's what they called it at that time. If your house catch a fire, throw your trunk out the window.
Yeah, very good, very good.
Well, they played blues at that time, like that. They played high society, numbers, like that. It was practically on the same order, like, fear on that.
Yeah. Did they ever play any routine or stuff just by the ear?
Oh yeah, yeah. The arrangement, this was occasionally at that time, or something that they wasn't so familiar with and when they learned it, but they played a lot of numbers without music.
Yeah, that's why I wondered how that...
Yeah, yeah.
Well, I was asking a little bit more about your Uncle Clay then. Do you remember which brass bands he played with? You mentioned your father came down and played with Onward and different bands.

Well, he played with the Salsa and occasionally with Moe's, every brass band in existence because he was a good drummer and anytime they had a chance to use him they would always try to get Clay Gile. Because Old Man Robichaud was the first man I understand that I heard that played a bass drum in New Orleans in the street. Joe Robichaud, he was a violin band.
Not a John Robichaud. John Robichaud. The old man, the violin. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Left-handed violin. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's right.
That's right. You know what town he came from? Is... John Robichaud? Yes.
If he...
I can't recall, but it's some country town, but I...
Somebody once said he came from Thibodeau. I wondered if you knew that he'd come from up there. Well, if he did, I don't remember. You didn't remember hearing about him at play.
But I know he come from some country. Yeah. Because when my uncle come to town, Clay Gile, and he played so much bass drum, he quit playing bass drum.
Robichaud did. That's right. Yeah.
That's right.
I suppose in those days like today they'd play with all the different bands. Oh yeah. That's right, that's right.

At that time, if you was good and you was idle and they needed a drummer, they would hire you, or any instrument. If it was a trumpet, clarinet, because musicians were scarce at that time, they wasn't plentiful like they are today.
You know if he played in any dance orchestras too, did you ever hear him play at dances?
Who is that?
Your uncle Clay.
No, he never did play nothing but brass bands. Just brass bands. My daddy played in the...
And of your other uncles, when they moved down, did they play in dance bands too?
No, they only played in brass bands.
And all your uncles moved down here, Albert?
That's right.
They all moved down here.
Yeah, that's right.
Oscar and Olivia.
Claire, that's right.
Olivia, yeah.
And they played in brass bands too?
Yeah, they all played in brass bands.
Did any of them play in dance bands besides your...
Daddy, no. None of them played in...
You would rate your uncle, and after your father you would say your uncle Clay was probably the...
The best.
And I thought he was the best known, I just wondered.
Yeah, that's right.
Because you should know, I mean... Yeah, that's right. They were all related to you, so you wouldn't have any bias. That's right. If you'd say so, he must be right.
Yeah.

Can you tell us a little bit more about your life then, when you started telling us, when we interrupted you about your uncles, when you studied with Mr. Chalier? Okay. Anything else about your lessons? Did you just work on snare drum, or did you have a whole drum set? How did he teach?
Oh, he teached me this with a snare drum.
Oh, by the way, did you have a drum pad any time? Or...
Yeah, when we went to lesson, you used a drum pad at lesson, but when the big band was together, well, everybody had the instruments. They would play the instruments.
Do you remember anything about how he would teach you in counting? If he... Did you count out loud, pat your foot, or any certain way of counting? Oh, yeah, yeah.
You had to count one, two. Slide your foot over. That's right. Yeah. He was very particular about your feet, working with your playing.
Yeah.

Because he said no man can ever play a music unless you use something. Every musician that's played, he got some way to count. Yeah. Some of them will sit and do like that to count. Shake their legs sideways. Yeah, something like that. Some of them, if they're not playing a blowing instrument, they'll hum to themselves. Yeah. You understand? You always, to keep in time, in some ways, about you, you have to keep the time, you know.
Is that what you use, Albert? You use your foot, do you?
The person who's playing a drummer. For a time, well, a drummer, he have to keep his time with the bass drum. That's his time, you see. That's his time. Okay, what do you do with the snare drum?
I mean, when you were learning, did you use your foot with Professor Chaline?
Oh yeah, he made you, yeah. You had to, I mean in counting, that's what you mean. Counting to start off and then you pat your feet. You had to, you see.
How long did you go to Professor Chaline?
I must have went to Chaline about two years. Two years. About two years.
All with the snare drum?

Always with the snare drum, yeah. You see, if you learn music, you wouldn't have to have all the drums. If he would have had orchestra, I would have to bring that out too, you see. But by him, I would have all the class to bring the instrument. It was so many that it would be a brass band. Yeah. You understand? Now, to play an orchestra, I mean you learn music, but the ideas and the feelings would have to come for you to make you be a good drummer. Because they had, many scholars went, didn't make it. As good a teacher as he was. Because if it's not in you.
You can't bring it out if it's not there to start.

But I mostly feel that that was born into me because I loved it. Well, when I got around my uncles and told them what I wanted to do, well they gave me encouragement, you know. And my little grandson reminded me of both of them that if they don't be drummers, I don't know why, because they pick up the sticks and use them they self and they can use, they're not tall enough to reach the small drum when it's on the stand, because I don't have a stand that can come down there, but they'll get on there and they'll stand up and play a good time. I can't even much show you, I'll set them drums up nine. A child is very funny when you want him to do something you won't do it, but they'll get there and they'll play and they should have more attention, but I figure they're quite young, yes, you know, but it's in them because anytime I get the drum they're ready, as ready as I am. Yeah, when we rehearsals here and set the drum up, they'll cry to get on there and play. And I mean, what they're making something, I don't mean that it's beating, it's you can tell it's something in them.
Some real rhythm to it.
Yeah, you understand? Yeah, so I think they will be the same as I was.
Yes, probably will be.
Yeah.

After you studied, say a couple of years, when did you start playing any jobs with the real band, not necessarily professional, or that is to get paid for, but when did you join any small group or brass band? Can you remember what you'd say is your first job or your first orchestra?

Well, after I got the drum, as I told you, my uncle got the drum from a forum shop. I was going to Lansing. I had a fellow come to bring society notice to my house. His name was Lawrence Randall. He said, I told him I had a drum. He said, well, I got a trumpet. I'm learning how to play music. He said, I'm thinking about going to Old Man Chalini. And I told him it was a good idea to go over there. And so he said, of course, I've been getting a little lessons from my uncle, Joe Nicholas. I said, yeah? I said, yeah. He said, what you say we make up a little band? I said, it's a good idea. I'd love it. So we formed a little band. Lawrence Randall, John Ankle, Gilbert, a fellow called Bush on banjo. So we would rehearse them twice a week. But the guys didn't have nerve enough to play. I felt to myself that I was about the strongest in the band. And I wasn't afraid to play, but they was. So a fellow told me about a job for Carnival. So I asked them, they told me, they said, oh man, we don't play good enough to go play no job. I said, we can make it. They said, no. So I had to give the job to somebody else and I didn't play either. So I met Lawrence Toker and he said, what you say if we make up a band? Well, he had nerve. He was Ambrose, the trombone player's nephew. So we made up a band with Lawrence Toker, Melvin Frank, Bill Hamilton. He was a banjo player. We made up a little band and we began to play together, or rehearsing, not playing a job. And a fellow named Harmon, he said that he had a house party. At that time they used to give a lot of house parties and lawn parties with short combination, like three pieces, some four pieces. He was a piano player. So you got Lawrence to play trumpet, me to play a drum. This was my first job of playing this lawn party. And we played together. The lady's name is Fenella. She have a son. He was a drummer Lionel, Torragander. I don't know if you heard of him. I've heard that name. Yeah, well, he got sick and he quit playing. But we played the job for her. And my first job was two and a half a man. A piece for each one of us. That was the job we played. So the following week, she decided to get Chris Kelly's band to play. So, well I was very interested in music. Anywhere I heard a band playing, I want to be there to learn as much as I could about playing. So on my way to the party, I meet Chris Kelly and Faisal going over to play. So he asked me to help carry his drum and that was just to my hand because I was very crazy about playing drum. So I told him on the way there, I said, I'm learning how to play drum myself. He said, yes, well that's all right. We get to the party, he plays about six or seven numbers. And he didn't say like this, say now, do you want to sit in? They used the phrase of, how's about resting me up? Let me see cuz, what you can do? Yeah. Well, I got on the drum, I started to play and so he appealed to Chris Kelly. He said, hey, he's a good little drummer. I said, where you live at? I live around the corner on Oberst Street. He said, yeah. He said, what you doing tomorrow night? I said, well, I'm not doing anything. He said, well, I think I can put you on a little job. He took me and Peter Pappy and Georgie Boyd. He was a great clarinet player. What did Pappy play? Banjo. This job was on Iberville and Marie for some Jewmakers. But he had a job at the Corporate Hall and one at the Economy Hall. That was on a Monday night because he was so popular at that time, he got a lot of jobs. Well, the drummer, Faiso, was playing with him. He put in with some other fellas and got some other band to go another job and he took me with him.
I don't want to interrupt you, but I'll never think of it again. How was Faiso as a drummer?
How? What style did he play? I never did. He was a great drummer. He was outstanding. I admired him a lot.
He was a natural born drummer. Did he have any special style, anything spectacular, anything different
that he did? Oh yeah, he really was a man that those blocks and could give you some of the perfect roles, rim shots on drums and placed. He was really outstanding. He was a great drummer.
Okay, you were talking about this job then with Chris. Yeah. That they put Faiso with another band.

On Marie and Iberville, they had a lot of Jewmakers coming into town at that time. And the woman that he was playing for, they had a lot of Jewmakers running with her. And so I understand, I didn't know at that time, that they were smuggling at the time. A lot of them. So the dance she'd give, would mostly be Jewmakers, they'd run on the ship. You see?
Yeah. And they was- Some of them would jump ship and stay there.

Yeah, they would. That's what they all would do. They had no passports. Some of them was stowed away. So we start to playing. So around 1130, Lauren Tokens, quite naturally, he followed me to play with Chris Kelly to see how I was going to make up. About 1130, Chris Kelly asked him to raise him up.
Yes, they're not.
So-
The police raided the place.

Yes, he said, stand on the side. I got on the side too. I'll go over this. The fella says, what's your name? My name is Sam Jones. He said, alright, you get on the side. I said, what's your name? I said, Albert Jarrell. He said, no, you get on this side. So, they arrested all the ones that didn't have their passport to send them back. That's where this song come out, I'm going home to Jamaica.
That's right.

That's right. We used to call it Going Home to Jamaica. So, from that night on, Chris Kelly decided to start to play, and I'm going home to Jamaica after that night. Because all those fellas, when they line them up and send them all back that didn't have their passport, back to Jamaica. So, this lady, she was so enthued over Lauren Stoker playing and being so young, that she sent for me to ask me could she get that little fella to play for her. So, that was one of the jobs that we stole away from Chris Kelly, because we started to play and we played several jobs and often for those people. And on those occasions, that's how I come to play with Chris Kelly and I played many advertisements, or truck jobs, or witness, or bands backing the tailgates together, what they call tailgate music, that we played a lot of those advertisements in those times. And I played often and on, it would take a very long time to tell that all the bands that I played with, I played occasionally with Kid Rene. His brother Joe was a drummer, but at times that he couldn't make it or his feet was hurting him because his feet was very bad.
Was he always pretty heavy? He was pretty heavy. Yeah, he always was.

Always was heavy. And he always suffered with his feet and occasionally I played with him. And the band from then on that we made up with Lawrence Stoker, Bill Hamilton the band, Bill Hamilton our first job with that band, we played out at Millenburg every night. Well, at that time Millenburg was wide open, they had what they used to call a little train that used to run out there, Smokey Mary.
Yeah, I've heard it, I never got to see it.
Yeah, we played out there every night for maybe about two years.
Was that open to the public or some private camp or what was it?
It was open to the public. The fellow was named Joe Barry, John Barry that had this nightclub like.
Sort of a nightclub, was it out over the water?

No, this one wasn't over the water. But I played occasionally when I remember could count 13 bands on the water playing in camps at that time. That's how it was great musicians. They would have some bands out there. Every band you could think of in York would have a camp playing.
Is that mostly on Sunday or weekends or at night?
Well mostly the weekends, but they had some of them run continually every night, like the one we played by, Barry Dot. Well he run every-
They have dancing there at your place?
Yeah, dancing and serving drinks just like-
Yeah, some regular nightclubs. Clubs, yeah.
But they said it was out at the lake but not on the water, the camp he had. And so many other camps, you know, that I played on the water.
Did you ever play with Buddy Petit or did you hear him very much?
Well I played a job, a couple of jobs with Buddy Petit. At the last, after he had left and come back to New Orleans.

Where'd he been? I think Sammy Penn or someone told him, Sammy used to play for him. I think he said he went across the lake or act like he lived there with some relatives. Was it across the lake, Mandeville or anything? Do you know where it was?
That's right, that's right, Mandeville. He went over there. After he left-
He left the city then for a while. You could say he moved away like that. Yeah, he did. I wondered.

I think he went further than Mandeville, but I think he went around Bonk, Louisiana and all different parts. But at the last he stood over there until he come a while and played here until he got sick and he died. Yeah. You know, but he had stood away but he was one of the greatest trumpet players in the staff going, not above the staff but in the staff. He made such nice, triple-tongued stuff, you know, right in-
Fast running.

That's right, in the stand. He was a real blues man who really could mix him up. But there's none beat Chris Kelly. You like Chris Kelly. He was great. I wish they had some record of him. Yes, too bad. Yeah, he- I don't think it's another man born that may have it, could play the blues like him. Chris- uh, Callie's love, Chris Kelly, could have been the composer of it. It was so great. He really was great. And he would use so much in his trumpet, could do so much with it. And he had a toilet flusher, he'd use it, put a mute in it, then he'd put that down, he'd get his durb, he'd put it in, then he'd use the rim of his durb, he was really great. And he'd go take it, put it up against the wall, and get different tones of it. Oh, I mean he was great, he was really great. A blues man he was. He would make everybody get happy.
Yeah.
Happy until they fight, when he played the blues. That's actually the facts.
Yeah.
That's actually the fact. They would start the fight. Uh, he had the blues like we played, and B-flat blues we played and make that stop.
Yeah, the holler blues they got off that. Yeah, the holler blues they got off that.
I mean when he played that, they would start the fight.
Really yell, huh? Yeah.
And Pork Chop Rag, he was real great on that. High Society, ice cream, he really can play those numbers. He played ice cream too?
Oh yeah, all those numbers, yeah. I never heard anybody do that until about 1945, when once Jim Robinson and George Lewis. Oh yeah, that's... They played it way back though.

Yeah, they did, yeah, they played that way back. Really, he was a real great musician. And I played with Silly Stamp Band, made up a band, not our, he made the band up. This was in around, last of 41. He had, things had gotten bad and he had broke up his band. He didn't have any band, Silly Stamp, Papa Silly Stamp.
Yeah, I remember, while he was out.

Yeah, he had broke up his band and took a job in 41, until the war was on, in that time, at the shipyard. And he made up a band, Ricard, a long time ago when he had his tuxedo band, was a trumpet player.
That's right, we talked about Ricard.

And Bill Mathias had played drum with Silly Stamp. He was a drummer a long time ago. When he made up this band, Ricard was playing bass with him. And Bill Mathias, did he playing drum, he was playing trombone with him. Albert Walters was playing trumpet. And Kit Clayton was playing with him. And we must have been up about six months. And I thought, when they knocked off at Higgins Shipyard, there were five and six hundred people would be docking off. And fellas coming through with their cars in a hurry. And they run into several fellas and knock them down, breaking their arms. And Silly Stamp was one of the ones that they run in and broke his leg. Well that broke up the band. After he was down with his leg, we had straight away and went to play with other different fellas. And Silly Stamp was out for maybe a year or so, and some fella said that he wanted to get a Dixieland band to play at the paddock. And he contacted Ricard. So Ricard saw Silly Stamp and instead of making an orchestra like he always had, he started playing Dixieland. So I mean some people think that Silly Stamp always was a Dixieland man, but he played classical music.
Yeah, some of his old records are a larger band. Yeah.

This in the later years, the last band that he got so famous was Dixieland was when he played on Boyfriend Street. Yeah. Because he was not a Dixieland man, but the average people think he was. But in the later years he began to play Dixieland because he never played unless he had two trumpets, a self-made tree, or either one trumpet player. But when he was on Boyfriend Street, he played one trumpet. That's the only time.
Very well. There, it's going again the machine stopped for a second. We were talking about Celestan and can you think of anything else that you went on from there after that group? After that group?

Well, I started playing with René Parker, a trumpet player. A fella, him and Big Fire, they call him, trombone player. They made up a band and they was going down the country, the Burris and all down in St. Bernard Parish. Mostly, that's the most of their work were down there playing. So, I got with that band. It was called Onida Jazz Band. And I drifted right along with them playing. I must have stayed with them about two years. The job was pretty good. And I did alright with them. And then I came back and thought that I could organize my own band.
Yeah, we're having trouble with this recorder now, but we'll try to finish up quickly so we'll get the rest of your life in here within five minutes if we can.

And I decided that I would make up a band of my own and I would be the manager of the band. So, I made up a band with Albert Walters, Frank Crump, Elwood Theodore. And we went along playing and doing nicely. And we must have stood together about three years. And finally, I meets up with Albert Boybanks, who I played with often and on. But Albert Boybanks made up a band and we begin to get together and play. And then out of Blue Sky one day, I meets a man they call Mr. Russell. And we're about that time that I came in here to hear you. Together, man. And we recorded some numbers from him. Can you recall the numbers?
Yeah, I guess the first date that you made was there over at Albert Burbank. Also some with Wooden Joe that year, 1945.
I did too, that's right. And Big Eye Louie and Joe Nicholas. That's the records we...

I wasn't, let's see, I don't believe you made the records quite at 1950. Yeah. Push it. Well, we were just saying you started recording there with Albert Burbank. And there was that date you made with Herb Moran. And then you made some with Wooden Joe that year. Yeah, I cannot...
It was 1949, I guess, when we made those records.
Yeah.
Well, I can recall... I could remember definite about those records made because you should know the year good. The last record we made, Bonk Johnson was very sick.
Yeah, that's right.
And we, you had to leave, we made a rehearsal and you couldn't finish recording. Because you had to go...
Yeah, the next day Bonk died and I went over there.
Yeah, yeah. You say you want to be there when he died. And...
That's when we were recording Wooden Joe out there in his backyard that night. That's right.
Remember that? That's right. That's right. I remember that very well. No.

Had you made any other records? We know you made that one little record that we just copied. You know, made that copy of the Four Piece Band with Burbank. Yeah. And let's see, who else was on it now? Talbot. Oh, yes.
Talbot. And Lester Lewis on piano, myself and Albert Buerbank.

Do you think about Lewis, can you, because of course we know, we didn't know Talbot, I knew him fairly well, but we never got to interview him of course. He died several years ago. Yeah. Can you tell us anything about Lewis?
Lewis the piano player? Yes. Well, he was a quite nice Dixieland piano player. And he gave it up. He stopped playing. But he was a very good piano player.
Wherever there was made that little record?

Well, these records were made in the Orleans Street Project, in a home. There was records that we tried to sell. We only wanted something to keep for our remembrance of our own musicians playing together. And the machine was for Lester Lewis. And we decided that we would make records. What made the records, I guess, come out of bed, not knowing how to buy the...
Well, I'll tell you, during the war they had those kind of glass-based things. I used those for a while. They wouldn't let you use aluminum. Yeah. That was probably... When was that made?
Well, that was made around 42. During the war, yeah.
That's right.
Around 42. That's when those records was made.
During the war you couldn't get the aluminum anymore. Yeah. Sometimes they had steel blanks, but sometimes glass. And that glass thing just broke on us.

Yeah, I had some other ones, but they all got broke. That one, that's why I was trying to get that one secured, so I would have something to remember. Yeah. But I'm sure Albert Boibank had some of them, but everybody mostly recorded what they wanted on the record to keep. Yeah. Yeah, and I'm sure Lester Lewis, Hanson Will Talbidge is dead. He's dead. I guess his wife may have, but I don't know. Well, look.
You know where his wife lives? He had that pressing plant I know up on Rambord Street. Did he live in that section? I wonder, do you know where she would be?
They were living right where the pressing shop was. That's what I thought. They live right now. But I don't know if she's still in that.
That's probably torn down, I think. Maybe, is it? Yeah, I don't know.
They've torn so much of that down.
That's right.
I can't remember. Well, I can't either, because they're tearing down so much. Well, of course. But she used to live there, I know, a while after he died, so I don't know if she's still living there.
Did you make any other records besides that?
Well, the record I made with King Collier, that's about the only records. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Opening and birth in Thibodaux, 1905
segments.summary: Interview opens at Giles's home on June 15, 1960; he gives his birthplace Thibodaux and birth date, November 27, 1905.

segments.title: Grandfather Napoleon Giles, Civil War drummer
segments.summary: Giles knows little of his grandfather Napoleon, a drummer in the Civil War, probably with the Union side; no dance music that he knows of.

segments.title: His father and the five drumming Giles brothers
segments.summary: His father Albert Giles Sr. died when he was about five, after setting up his drums for him; the five brothers (Clay, Oscar, Olivier, Major, Albert) were all drummers from Thibodaux.

segments.title: Uncles in New Orleans brass bands and Joe Gabriel's Thibodaux band
segments.summary: His father played in Joe Gabriel's band; the uncles moved to New Orleans, Clay with the Excelsior Brass Band, Oscar and Olivier with Onward.

segments.title: His father's homemade drum set and what became of it
segments.summary: Describes his father's wooden trap pedal, Chinese cymbals, blocks and cowbells; his mother got rid of the set and he later bought his own.

segments.title: Moving to New Orleans and buying his first drums
segments.summary: He moved to New Orleans at about 16, lived with his grandmother and Uncle Oscar, and bought a $25 secondhand set from a pawnshop with wages from a $9-a-week job.

segments.title: Professor Chaligny's lessons and big student band
segments.summary: Uncle Clay took him to Old Man Chaligny, who taught at his St. Claude Street home for 25 cents and ran a large scholars' band that rehearsed at a hall.

segments.title: Chaligny as trumpeter and bandleader
segments.summary: Chaligny had retired from playing by then; he was a trumpeter and reportedly once had his own brass band.

segments.title: Uncle Clay Giles: drummer, comedian and buck dancer
segments.summary: Clay was the best of the brothers after his father; a showman and soft-shoe dancer who played vaudeville but would not travel with shows, and played brass bands in New Orleans.

segments.title: Joe Gabriel's Thibodaux brass and dance band
segments.summary: Joe Gabriel, a violinist, led a brass band and an eight-piece dance orchestra sounding like the Piron band.

segments.title: Repertoire of the Thibodaux dance bands
segments.summary: They played waltzes, quadrilles, blues and stock arrangements, including 'Ho Alley Ho' and High Society, and many numbers by ear.

segments.title: Clay Giles in the brass bands, and Robichaux's bass drum
segments.summary: Clay played every brass band in town; John Robichaux was the first to play bass drum in the street; the uncles played only brass bands.

segments.title: How Chaligny taught: snare, counting and keeping time; drumming in the family
segments.summary: Two years of snare drum with a pad, counting aloud and patting the foot; time must come from within the player. He feels drumming was born in him and sees it in his grandsons.

segments.title: First bands, first lawn-party job, and sitting in with Chris Kelly
segments.summary: A band with Lawrence Randall was too timid to play; he formed one with Lawrence Toker, played a lawn party for two and a half dollars, then sat in with Chris Kelly and got hired.

segments.title: Drummer Faiso's style
segments.summary: Giles admired Kelly's drummer Faiso as outstanding on blocks, rolls and rim shots.

segments.title: Jamaican ship-jumpers' dance raid, tailgate jobs, Kid Rena
segments.summary: Police raided a dance for Jamaican ship jumpers, inspiring 'Going Home to Jamaica'; Giles took the job from Kelly, played tailgate ads and subbed for Joe Rena.

segments.title: Two years at Milneburg with Lawrence Toker and Bill Hamilton
segments.summary: His band played nightly for about two years at John Barry's Milneburg club, reached by Smokey Mary, among camps on the lake.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's later years
segments.summary: Giles played a couple of jobs with Petit after he returned from across the lake; he praised Petit's triple-tonguing trumpet.

segments.title: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter
segments.summary: He considers no one played the blues like Kelly, who used plumber's-plunger and derby mutes and drew crowds to fights; also Pork Chop Rag and High Society.

segments.title: Celestin's wartime band and his later Dixieland turn
segments.summary: In 1941 Celestin, after a shipyard job and a broken leg, formed a band with Ricard Alexis, Albert Walters and others; Giles says Celestin was not originally a Dixieland man.

segments.title: Playing with Rene Parker, then leading his own band
segments.summary: Two years with Rene Parker's band in St. Bernard Parish, then his own band with Albert Walters, Frank Crump and Elwood Theodore for about three years.

segments.title: Meeting Bill Russell and recording with Burbank, Wooden Joe and others
segments.summary: Recalls recordings with Albert Burbank, Herb Morand, Wooden Joe, Big Eye Louis and Joe Nicholas around 1949, ending around Bunk Johnson's last illness.

segments.title: Glass-disc home recording with Burbank, Talbot and Lester Lewis
segments.summary: A four-piece home recording made during the war, with glass blanks, in the Orleans Street project; Lewis's piano and where Talbot's widow might live.

segments.title: Other records and closing
segments.summary: The only other record he made was with King Collier.
